To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
temporal changes in gene expression of mammalian neural precursor cells are independent of cell-cycle progression.
the temporal identity of apical progenitors is controlled by cell-cycle independent mechanisms.

the timing mechanisms that control the identity of neural progenitor cells are cell-cycle independent and that the identity of these cells is controlled by cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that generate neuronal diversity in the mammalian cortex.
how the identity of neural progenitor cells changes over time, which is an important question in neuroscience.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of neural circuits in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
temporal transitions in AP gene identity occur during cell-cycle arrest, and are not affected by Notch activity.
the cell cycle does not regulate the temporal identity of neural progenitors.
cell-cycle arrest of apical progenitor cells (APCs) does not alter their identity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
temporal transitions of APs are independent of cell cycle progression, and that the timing mechanisms for APs are different from those of Drosophila neuroblasts.

temporal changes in the identity of mammalian apical neural progenitors occur independently of the cell cycle and are not driven by Notch signaling, but rather, are controlled by cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic factors.
cell cycle progression does not play a role in the temporal identity of APs, but rather, cell-intrinsic mechanisms and extrinsic signals do.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cell-cycle progression is dispensable for the generation of neuronal diversity in the cerebral cortex.
the timing mechanism controlling temporal identity of mammal neural progenitor cells functions independently of cell-cycle and Notch signaling.
cell-cycle arrest does not prevent APs from changing their temporal identity and acquiring the correct laminar fating of their descendant neurons.
